fixes.explanation: No treaty in this message, baker. Amaziah, king of Judah, just says, “Come, let us meet face to face…” (2 Chronicles 25:17). He doesn't mention a deal or a signing. It's a short invitation, nothing more.

Not that one, friend. Amaziah asks for no silver and no gold. He only says, “Come, let us meet face to face…” (2 Chronicles 25:17). The gold does change hands later, but it leaves Jerusalem, and that's not a good day for Judah.

Yes, baker. Jehoash, king of Israel, says, “Then a wild beast in Lebanon came along and trampled the thistle.” (2 Chronicles 25:18). Short story, and the ending is rough on the thistle. That thistle went in asking for a wedding and came out flat.
Good guess, but that's not how Jehoash tells it. The text says a wild beast came along and trampled the thistle (2 Chronicles 25:18). The beast does the trampling, not the cedar.

True, baker. Jehoash says, “You have said, ‘Look, I have defeated Edom,’ and your heart has become proud and boastful.” (2 Chronicles 25:19). He doesn't dance around it. He repeats Amaziah's own words about Edom and then says his heart has become proud and boastful.

It's true, friend. Jehoash tells Amaziah, “…your heart has become proud and boastful.” (2 Chronicles 25:19). He says it right after repeating Amaziah's own words about defeating Edom. No hint-dropping here. He says it plainly in his reply.
Home it is, baker. Jehoash says, “Now stay at home.” (2 Chronicles 25:19). Four words and a whole lot of sense. I stayed put in a junk drawer for years, so trust me, it can be done.

Right, baker. Jehoash says, “Why should you stir up trouble so that you fall—you and Judah with you?” (2 Chronicles 25:19). Amaziah isn't the only one in that warning, because Judah is named right alongside him. That's the part that stings.

That's the reason, baker. The writer says this had come from God “…because they had sought the gods of Edom.” (2 Chronicles 25:20). Edom, the nation Amaziah says he defeated, had gods of its own, and Judah went looking to them. The text gives the reason plainly, so I won't add one.

Right, baker. Jehoash captured Amaziah at Beth-shemesh, and the text says it happened “There at Beth-shemesh…” (2 Chronicles 25:23). The army scatters, but Amaziah is captured. He asked for a face to face meeting, and he got one.

Not guards, friend. The text says Jehoash “…broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate—a section of four hundred cubits.” (2 Chronicles 25:23). He breaks the wall down, and the text never mentions guards.

Not all of it stays standing, baker. Jehoash “…broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate—a section of four hundred cubits.” (2 Chronicles 25:23). It isn't the whole wall, but it's a big section, and it comes down.

Hostages, baker. The text says Jehoash took the gold, the silver and the articles, “…as well as some hostages.” (2 Chronicles 25:24). Then he returned to Samaria. He took treasure from the house of God and the royal palace treasuries, and people went with him too.

Not Bethel, baker. Amaziah “…fled to Lachish.” (2 Chronicles 25:27). A conspiracy had been formed against him in Jerusalem, and the men sent after him still reach him there. It's a quiet, heavy part of the story.
